title: Attention, always
hookLine: once you relax your attention, don't think you can pick it back up whenever you like

lines: TWENTY MINUTES LATER: A FRYING PAN.
cards: You pick up your phone to check one thing, the weather. Twenty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusted frying pan, with no memory of deciding to. You never checked the weather.
Epictetus knew this slide, without the phone.
Near the end of the Discourses, book four, chapter twelve, there's a short, sharp talk about what happens when you let your attention go, and why getting it back is harder than it looks.

teach.b: Prosochē is Greek for attention, from a verb meaning to hold toward: to hold the mind toward something. For Epictetus it's the watchfulness under every other practice.

You can't sort what's yours from what isn't if you aren't paying attention when the moment comes. His warning: when you relax your attention for a while, don't imagine you can pick it back up whenever you like.

teach.h: A SLIP TODAY MAKES TOMORROW'S EASIER.
teach.b: Today's slip makes tomorrow's easier. A habit of not attending forms quietly, and then you're always putting it off. Tomorrow I'll be careful, people say.
Which means, he points out, that today you won't be. Nothing gets done well without attention, he says, not by the carpenter, not by the person steering a ship.

teach.h: NO CRAFT IS DONE HALF ASLEEP.
teach.b: Why would living well be the one craft you could do half asleep? Then the honest part.
Can anyone be faultless? No, Epictetus says plainly. What is possible is to keep straining toward not making mistakes.
If, by never letting attention go completely, we avoid even a few faults, that's worth having. He isn't asking for perfection. He's asking you to keep showing up to your own life.
Later, some Christian monastic writers used prosochē as one of their words for watchfulness of the heart: the same small word, down a different road. Attention isn't something you finish.
You return to it, and the returning is the practice.

how: Stoic practice includes prosochē, a steady watchfulness over one's own judgments and actions, renewed many times a day whenever attention slips.

o: a perfect focus that never slips at all
attention: holding the mind toward what's here
a careful plan for being better tomorrow

s: Epictetus expects his students never to make mistakes
he says being faultless isn't possible; keep straining toward it anyway.
he says you can't always pick attention back up whenever you like
today's slip makes tomorrow's easier; a habit of inattention forms.
some later Christian monks also used the word prosochē
some later Christian monastic writers used it for watchfulness of the heart.

games.q: you've drifted all morning. a voice in your head says: today's gone, start fresh tomorrow. what does Epictetus say?
o: tomorrow I'll be careful means today you won't be. come back now.
punish yourself so it doesn't happen again.
games.why: in book four, chapter twelve, he warns that putting attention off to tomorrow just builds the habit of putting it off.

practice: Choose one small task you can do right now, folding a shirt, washing a cup, or simply breathing, and give it all of you: the fabric, the water, the air.
When your mind wanders, and it will, notice where it went and bring it back gently, without scolding. Each return is a rep.

wordCard.voice: Prosochē. Greek for attention, holding the mind toward what's in front of you; for Epictetus, the watchfulness every other practice depends on. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: attention, from prosechein, to hold the mind toward; a core Stoic practice.

carryVoice: Your line: attention. Not faultless, just always coming back to what is in front of you. Day four hundred twenty-nine, done.
